newsitem.title: USA: Court paves way for Oklahoma trial to start.
newsitem.headline: Court paves way for Oklahoma trial to start.

text.p: A federal appeals court on Friday denied three requests by Oklahoma City bombing defendant Timothy McVeigh to postpone his trial, clearing the way for it to start as scheduled on Monday.
The court said that the issues raised by McVeigh's lawyers can be taken up if he is convicted.

McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols are charged in the April 19, 1995 bombing which killed 168 people. The attack on Oklahoma City's Alfred P. Murrah federal building was the largest such assault ever on U.S. soil.
The date for Nichols' trial has not yet been determined.

The court said McVeigh's attorneys were "premature" in seeking a delay on grounds of prejudicial pre-trial publicity linked to two reports published in the Dallas Morning News and Playboy Magazine containing purported confessions by McVeigh.
McVeigh's lawyers had complained that U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch was so intent on starting the trial on time that he was willing to sacrifice McVeigh's right to a fair trial.

McVeigh's lawyers said the Dallas Morning News article was "devastating" and that "any flicker of hope that an impartial jury could be selected ... was finally extinguished" when the Playboy article was published on the Internet.
McVeigh's lawyers said answers given by prospective jurors showed McVeigh will not be able to get a fair trial.
"The responses contained within the juror questionnaires demonstrate that Mr. McVeigh simply cannot receive a fair trial under the circumstances as they presently exist," the lawyers said.

Some 1,000 notices went out to prospective jurors in Denver and 22 surrounding counties. Several hundred of them met with the judge and attorneys for both sides on March 19 where they filled out a questionnaire.
McVeigh's lawyers said that after they read the answers their fears were confirmed and that they asked the judge on Tuesday to delay the trial.
However, the judge refused their motion in a closed door hearing on Thursday, prompting them to rush to the appeals court after normal closing hours.
The appeal court also denied a request made on Tuesday to delay the trial to allow the court to consider a defence request for classified intelligence date from prosecutors.
The defence said it needed the material to investigate its theory that a foreign government, possibly Iraq, may have planned the bombing.
In a filing with the appeals court, prosecutors said the defence theory "reads like a bad Hollywood script."

The appeals court also dismissed a request, filed on Wednesday, to delay the trial to give McVeigh an opportunity to challenge the constitutionality of a new law allowing victims to view the proceedings and testify at a penalty phase of the trial if McVeigh is convicted.
All three requests were petitions for extraordinary remedies, which are seldom granted.
McVeigh's attorneys said the trial judge's "insistence that Mr. McVeigh's trial begin as scheduled, come hell or high water, has been obvious for some time."
